As he noted how coddled kids were nowadays compared with older generations, area grandfather Hank Hayes recalled Friday that when he was young, he had to evolve legs to get to school. “Back in my day, if you wanted an education, you had to crawl out of the ocean on your fins until you gradually developed limb-like structures that allowed you to move across land,” said Hayes, who added that unlike his grandkids, he’d had to wake up each morning at 6 a.m., flop himself from the sea onto a beach, and drag himself to class using nothing but his webbed phalanges. “Kids these days can just go to school without having to worry about predators, mass extinctions, or adapting their bodies to breathe oxygen as they lose their residual gills. But I worked hard to walk upright. I didn’t even have weight-bearing limbs until I was in college!” Hayes went on to state that even though they might not survive, today’s young people could learn a lot by experiencing natural selection.
posts.hd: Grandpa recalls evolving legs to get to school

🏁 Grace Potter and the Trespassers | Thursday, January 14 at the Paramount Theatre in Rutland, VT 📢 On sale now 🤘 _ With her new album Trespasser, Grace Potter introduces a beautifully unruly cast of characters who step into forbidden spaces with absolute abandon. As the spiritual sequel to 2023’s Mother Road, the four-time Grammy nominee’s seventh studio LP continues the kaleidoscopic storyline drawn from bi-coastal life between Topanga Canyon, CA and the family farm in her native Vermont (a road-trip journey she’s made eight times in the last five years, usually on her own). Trespasser ultimately lights the way toward a more unbound and expansive means of moving through the world.

posts.c: 🪐 Saturnalia | Friday, December 18 📢 On sale now 🤘 _ Saturnalia is an ancient Roman festival celebrated around the winter solstice in honor of the god Saturn. Its true origin is somewhat mysterious, but it is clear that its purpose was to call back the Golden Age, a time over which Saturn, god of time, abundance, and freedom ruled. On December 18th, in Higher Ground’s Showcase Lounge, an eclectic group of Vermont creatives will gather to showcase movement, music, and art with a nod to this ancient tradition. The innovative and immersive format could be compared to Cirque du Soleil meets House of Yes with a Vermont DIY spirit; guests will be entertained by the area’s finest pole dancers, aerialists, and movement artists, abstract projections and light-based installations, and curated sets by DJs who are lighting up Burlington’s underground electronic music scene. This story was researched and written through ProPublica’s Local Reporting Network, in which the award-winning investigative nonprofit is teaming up with Seven Days on a yearlong project. posts.c: Last week we finished up our first adult Learn to Ride class! This free multi week collaboration between Old Spokes Home and Local Motion offered instruction for folks learning to ride for the first time, and for others needing a refresher. This class contributes to Old Spokes Home's overall mission of removing barriers to make bikes work for everyone. It also aligns perfectly with Local Motion's mission of making it safe, accessible, and fun for everyone to bike, walk, and roll in Vermont. The ability to ride a bike, and to ride it safely, opens up opportunities at any age! This class eases students into riding by focusing on balance first. Bikes without cranks and pedals act as adult striders, and as students became more comfortable they work up to bikes with pedals. We'll be offering more FREE adult Learn to Ride classes in the spring!

Saving a 136-year-old cast iron tub 🛁✨ Homeowners Harley and Ethan wanted to keep the original tub that came with the house, so @kevinoconnortoh and @dettmore101 took on the refinish together. Part 1: Stripping Suited up with respirators, since old paint can be lead-based Troweled on a ¼” layer of stripper paste Covered it with craft paper to keep it wet Let it work for 24 hours Bagged and sealed the paint, then scraped down to bare metal Part 2: Buffing + Painting Primed and sanded the outside Buffed the inside enamel with cerium oxide (a glass polish) and water Rinsed it, and the shine was back Flipped the tub and rolled on a matte black and white finish The matte finish hides the pitting and ties in with the tile Ready for another 130 years 🙌 📺 Watch today on @pbs (check local listings), and stream free Monday on @therokuchannel #TOHEssexCo #ThisOldHouse #TubRefinish #homeimprovement #beforeandafter
posts.cp: Saving a 136-year-old cast iron tub

posts.c: Lava is hot. We thought you should know. We’ve been asked to elaborate. Fine. Lava is hot. It’s like making a grilled cheese, except the pan is a volcano on fire. Too much? Is it getting hot in here? Take two. Erupting lava at Hawaiʻi’s Kīlauea Volcano typically reaches around 2,100°F (1,150°C). That’s hot enough to turn rock into a glowing river of molten material. It’s also hot enough that getting too close can be extremely dangerous. Lava the view from a safe, designated viewing area, follow park guidance, and please resist the urge to find out just how hot it is firsthand. Some things are better left untouched. Lava is very high on that list. Has anyone touched lava lately? That’s not a question for you. We’re getting ahead of your questions. The answer, not that we know of. This is just a a friendly reminder to avoid any incidents. Plus even though lava is hot stuff, the pics are pretty cool to look at! NPS Photos: @hawaiivolcanoesnps /J. Wei

posts.c: Sports and recreation can be a way to embrace the winter — to meet the season on its own snowy, icy terms. For the Central Vermont Pioneers sled hockey club, leaning in is the essence of the sport, an exhilarating athletic activity requiring uncommon balance, core strength, eye-hand coordination and teamwork. And sleds. And hockey sticks with metal spikes. Bring it on, winter. Sled hockey — also known as sledge hockey or para ice hockey — is an adaptive sport popular among athletes with disabilities that limit lower-body mobility. Players sit in metal sleds that rest upon two blades mounted under a bucket seat. They propel themselves by digging into the ice with teeth-like metal picks on the butt ends of two hockey sticks, one for each hand. The sticks are roughly one-third the length of standard nonadaptive hockey sticks. Play can be fast-paced, physical and, according to Pioneers captain Jacob “Jake” Lavigne, “awkward.” Through sled hockey, Pioneers players have found a sense of belo

posts.c: Rifle season opens this Saturday, and before everyone heads out into the woods, we wanted to help everyone have a safe and successful hunt by addressing a few Frequently Asked Questions we’ve been receiving: Q: Can I still hunt archery during rifle season? A: Rifle season & archery season are two completely separate seasons, each with their own regulations, with dates that overlap. Follow the regulations based on type of hunting you want to do, and which tags you have. For example, if a hunter wants to take a deer using their rifle tag, then they will hunt under rifle season regulations. If they’d like to take a deer using their archery tag, then they would hunt with their bow and under archery season regulations. Q: If a hunter is archery hunting, can they take an antlerless deer anywhere in the state? A: Yes, the archery season allows you to take an antlerless deer statewide. The hunter would tag with their archery tag and follow all archery regulations. Q: If a hunter has an antlerl

posts.c: Rowan Atkinson, the man behind Mr. Bean, has a master’s degree in electrical engineering from Oxford University! Despite playing one of television’s most hilariously clueless characters, Atkinson is academically accomplished and developed his famous comedy persona while studying at Oxford. Even more surprisingly, Mr. Bean speaks very little, yet the character became a worldwide sensation, proving that physical comedy can transcend language barriers. In 2001, Atkinson reportedly helped save a private plane after its pilot fainted during a flight in Kenya. He briefly took control of the aircraft while his wife tried to revive the pilot, who eventually regained consciousness and landed safely. Atkinson is also a passionate car enthusiast who once owned a McLaren F1, which he crashed twice before selling it for a reported £8 million in 2015. Like this content? posts.c: Burying food scraps in your garden sounds like an easy way to feed your plants, but there’s a little more soil science involved than you might think. Organic matter doesn’t become plant food overnight. Soil microbes, fungi, and other decomposers have to break it down first, converting complex organic compounds into simpler nutrients that plant roots can eventually absorb. Here’s the catch: decomposition takes time, and fresh organic materials can temporarily tie up nutrients as microbes consume them to do their work. Depending on the material, its carbon-to-nitrogen ratio, and how quickly it breaks down, burying food scraps can actually delay nutrient availability rather than give plants an immediate boost. Materials like raw animal tissue also need time to decompose, which can make nutrient release unpredictable. posts.c: A man was once classified as a dwarf and later grew so tall that he became a giant! Adam Rainer, born in Austria in 1899, is the only documented person in medical history to have been classified as both a dwarf and a giant. At age 21, he stood just 4 feet 0.25 inches (122 cm) tall. However, a rare condition involving his pituitary gland triggered extraordinary growth, and by age 51, he had reached approximately 7 feet 8 inches (234 cm). Even more astonishing, Rainer continued growing well into adulthood, long after most people’s bones stop lengthening. His dramatic growth was accompanied by serious health complications, including spinal curvature, deteriorating eyesight, and difficulty walking. He eventually became bedridden and died in 1950, leaving behind one of the most extraordinary medical cases ever recorded. Like this content? Follow us for more @dadsaysjokes ❤️

posts.c: Cheetah lookout 🐆 "It was a very windy morning in the Serengeti. I set out with my guests with low expectations of finding some cats on the kopjes as in my experience I had noted that when the wind is too strong, they don’t particularly like to be out on the rocks, especially in the early mornings. They are often happy to just lie down in the middle of the grasslands. As we drove through magnificent granite formations, some enormous, rising into the sky like carefully crafter sculptures, I noticed a lone cheetah walking in the tall grass, heading in the direction of a small characteristic rock, formed by a round boulder resting on a sort of pedestal. We immediately parked next to the rock as the cheetah jumped on it, looked around for probably less than five seconds and then descended again. It is the power of photography to render eternal the beauty and the emotions of what is actually a fleeting moment." - Federico Veronesi (@federico_veronesi) This week's #WPY62 guest is our Wildlif

posts.c: We’re travelling with Doodle again, and again with @akasaair 🐶✈️ After our last flight, I got so many DMs asking how I prepare Doodle, crate train him, which crate we use and what I pack, so here’s everything I do before we fly. Honestly, most of the preparation happens before you even reach the airport. 🐾 Crate prep: I keep Doodle’s crate around for a few days before the flight so he can get comfortable going in, chilling and sleeping in it. 📦 Right-size crate: Doodle’s crate is 32 inches. Make sure your pet can comfortably stand, turn around and lie down. I also use a crate with removable wheels for easier handling. 🧸 Familiar comforts: His familiar comforter and favourite toy always go inside, something that smells like home helps him feel more settled. posts.c: Have you discovered this North Bennington treasure yet? @parkmccullough is one of the most beautifully preserved Victorian mansions in New England; a grand 1864 estate surrounded by rolling lawns, towering trees, and miles of peaceful walking trails. Even if the mansion is closed for the season, the grounds are open year-round, and they’re stunning in every kind of weather. It’s one of my favorite places to wander with our dogs, soak up a little local history, and bring out-of-state visitors when we want to show off a true Vermont gem. The Mile-Around Woods trail starts right on the property, making it the perfect spot for an adventurous afternoon that blends nature with history. The house reopens for tours on summer weekends and stays open through fall foliage, with special events that make the property feel even more magical. If you’ve been, what’s your favorite part of the estate? If not… add this one to your list. Share this with someone who wants a peaceful walk steeped in hstory,

posts.c: Hey, give that back! 🚨 Toco toucans normally eat fruit, but as omnivores they can eat the eggs and chicks of other birds when the opportunity arises. Julius Dadalti (@juliusdadalti) was able to catch the moment that one toucan made off with the egg of a great kiskadee, with its owners in hot pursuit. Julius had seen the toucan eating eggs at the nest before it took off into the forest with one delicately clasped in its large bill. While it’s not certain what became of the egg, the toucan might have taken it to feed its own chicks. 📸 ‘Egg Thief’ was highly commended in the Behaviour: Birds category of this year's Wildlife Photographer of the Year. If you’ve enjoyed Julius’ work, get excited as he’ll be taking part in our guest series next week – so stay tuned! To see more fascinating snapshots of the natural world, book your tickets for #WPY62 now via the link in our bio. 💚 #WPY #WildlifePhotographerOfTheYear #WildlifePhotography #NaturePhotography #NaturalHistoryMuseum #Brazil #Toucan

posts.c: When Yellowstone was established in 1872, the National Park Service did not yet exist (and wouldn't until 1916). The park's first civilian superintendents lacked experience, funds, and a workforce to protect the park from exploitation. Eventually, Company M, First U.S. Cavalry of Ft. Custer, Montana Territory, answered the call to come to Yellowstone in 1886. This started the 30+ years of military protection of Yellowstone National Park. From the beginnings of Yellowstone to modern day, and all the time in between, we thank those who have served in the U.S. Armed Forces and continue to serve in a different uniform for the NPS. #VeteransDay 👉 Take a walking tour of the Fort Yellowstone Historic District or check out our virtual tour to learn more: https://www.nps.gov/thingstodo/yell-tour-fort-yellowstone.htm (available in our bio) Photos (from the NPS Historical Archive and Jacob W. Frank): 1. Mounted cavalry drill on Fort Yellowstone's Parade Ground in Mammoth Hot Springs (c. 1910) 2.

posts.c: Health insurance premiums for Vermont teachers are poised to see their smallest increase in nearly two decades. The Vermont Education Health Initiative, a self-insured trust that manages health benefits for about 33,000 school employees and their families, announced proposed premium hikes late last month that will average 2.5% next school year. That’s the smallest increase since the 2009-2010 school year. The health trust’s premium increases offer further evidence that Vermont’s laser focus on bringing down prices — particularly at hospitals — is mitigating a healthcare affordability crisis that at one point threatened to bankrupt the state’s largest insurer. Healthcare utilization appears to be cooling somewhat, according to VEHI officials. But the primary driver behind more reasonable premium increases is the underlying cost of care. Read the full story at the link in our bio. Photo by April McCullum/Vermont Public.

posts.c: "I was in the stunning Serengeti NP in Tanzania, one hot February in 2019, driving around on my own on a break between safaris. I left camp with a vague plan to check what was going on at one particular kopje. When I reached there I didn’t find anything so I made my way to this other kopje where lions often hang-out. Just as I pulled up, a lioness woke up and walked to the ledge of the rocky outcrop, immediately followed by the male. She stopped to look around and he reached her, for a split second they stood perfectly aligned, side by side, looking in the same direction, their bodies merging one into the other. I took the photographs and kept on following them as they descended the rock and continued their honeymoon in the grass. It was only later when I got home and converted the image in black and white that the power of this image was fully revealed. posts.c: Between teaching painting, communications work, and the many moving parts of public art, studio has been a hard reach, but I’m always (over and over) finding my way back to my own studio practice. Sometimes the studio itself feels like a habit I have fallen out of; the space is so overwhelming when I return, I don’t know where to start. posts.c: Powering up research!☀️⚡ Last week, space station astronauts installed the eighth and final roll-out solar array (ROSA), completing a five-year power upgrade. Roll-out solar arrays have a lightweight and compact design that launches as a cylinder and unfurls like a yoga mat after installation. Despite being about half the size of the legacy arrays, the eight additional roll-out solar arrays boost the station’s power generation by more than 160 kilowatts. Together, the arrays provide increased power for daily operations and hundreds of research investigations that benefit humanity and support future exploration missions. Following prior testing on space station, the roll-out solar arrays have also been used on NASA’s Dart mission, showcasing space station’s essential role as a testbed for the technologies needed for expeditions beyond Earth’s orbit.

posts.c: Calling all teachers, educators and homeschoolers: now is the time to sign up for Scat & Tracks! This fun, educational program is designed to get students from kindergarten through eighth grade outside and exploring Vermont's landscapes and local wildlife by giving educators the plans and support they need to lead nature hikes on school or nearby grounds. Each week for four weeks, students will watch a pre-recorded video that focuses on one Vermont species and covers topics such as habitat, lifecycle and natural history facts. After the video, the students head outside with their teacher to look for the appropriate habitat of the animal that was featured, paying close attention to scat, tracks, and other signs of the critter. This year's featured species includes moose, long-tailed weasel, eastern cottontail, and red fox! The deadline to register is December 15th. Don't wait! Sign up today at https://www.vtfishandwildlife.com/learn-more/conservation-education/scat-and-tracks-program

posts.c: Asparagus is a perennial because it has an underground storage system that keeps it coming back year after year. The crown, a cluster of buds and roots just below the soil, stores carbohydrates that fuel new spear growth every spring. Its deep, established root system also helps the plant access water and nutrients beyond the reach of many shallow-rooted vegetables. Here’s the interesting part: those feathery ferns aren’t just extra foliage. They’re the plant’s solar panels. Through photosynthesis, they capture sunlight and convert it into sugars, which are transported down to the crown and stored as energy reserves. The more energy the crown accumulates during the growing season, the more resources it has to produce healthy spears in the seasons ahead. That’s why harvesting asparagus too early can set the plant back. Every spear you cut is a potential fern that could have been producing energy for the underground crown. Letting those spears mature allows the plant to build the reserve

posts.c: Across the National Park System, forts, battlefields, historic homes and coastal defenses preserve the places where military history unfolded, and the stories of the people who lived it. At Minute Man National Historical Park, follow the route where the opening battles of the American Revolution began. At Fort McHenry National Monument & Historic Shrine, discover the story behind the flag that inspired “The Star-Spangled Banner.” And at Pearl Harbor National Memorial, remember the lives forever changed by the events of December 7, 1941. From Revolutionary War battlefields to World War II installations and Cold War defenses, these places connect us to generations of service, sacrifice and the lasting impact of conflict. posts.c: On display at the Visitor Center this month: bright and evocative Vermont landscape paintings from @laurelwatersart. Stop by and admire these swirling, colorful original paintings and prints. Laurel is a local artist inspired by nature. She began her adult life in Vermont working in the Green Mountains as a wilderness therapy guide. posts.c: Have you ever wondered how a forest changes over its lifetime? Biodiverse forest communities depend on interconnected forest habitats that vary in age and forest structure. Early successional, or young forests, like the one illustrated here feature canopy gaps that allow sunlight to reach the forest floor. These gaps are created by forest disturbances, including natural events like windstorms as well as carefully planned forest management. Removing a few trees creates space and opportunity for a new generation of trees and diverse communities of plants, fungi, and wildlife. These changes can happen all at once or gradually over time and can affect just a small area or several acres. Get started fostering biodiversity in your forest. Check out the @uvmextforestry's new Forest Biodiversity website for educational guides and stewardship resources. Developed in partnership with @audubonvermont, @vtcoverts, Vermont Biodiversity Alliance, @vtforestsparksrecreation, and @vwatreefarm . 🔗Link i

posts.c: Earth’s protective ozone layer is still on track for long-term recovery, despite a larger Antarctic ozone hole this year. The 2026 ozone hole is the 7th-largest ozone hole since NASA began tracking it in 1979. This year, the ozone hole reached its maximum extent of 10.5 million square miles on September 18. However, the ozone hole could have been 1 to 2 million square miles larger if ozone-depleting substances were as prevalent in the atmosphere today as they were two decades ago. posts.c: We have Chrysanthemum Festival down to a science. 👉 Swipe to find out how our growers perfected their techniques to create a display that builds on centuries of history and decades of innovation. Some of our chrysanthemum forms require a little tough horticultural love! During training, our gardeners allow the plants to wilt slightly, making their stems more pliable so they can be carefully shaped around custom metal frameworks. (There are very few plants that are willing to grow and bloom in a spiral!) Mums are short-day plants, meaning they naturally begin to develop flower buds as the nights grow longer in the fall. But at Longwood, we use a little horticultural know-how to time their blooms just right for Chrysanthemum Festival. By carefully controlling their exposure to light and darkness, our growers can encourage the plants to bloom right on schedule. Many of our mum forms are grafted onto Artemisia rootstock to benefit from its strong root system and resistance to summer heat,

When thinking about how I wanted to support our community during my year of service, I thought how can I support the ultimate supporters? Mothers. posts.c: On National Bison Day, we celebrate one of America’s most iconic animals and a powerful symbol of strength and resilience. Once reduced to fewer than 1,000 individuals, bison have made a remarkable comeback thanks to decades of dedicated conservation efforts. Today, the National Park Service supports 19 bison herds across 12 states, helping ensure these magnificent animals continue to roam the landscape. Of course, majestic doesn’t mean approachable. Bison are wild, unpredictable, and considerably less interested in meeting you than you might be in meeting them. No matter how calm or cow-like they appear, always stay at least 25 yards away. Finally, if you encounter bison on the road, remember: they’re in no hurry, and your schedule is not their concern. Slow down, stay in your vehicle, and patiently wait for them to move along. Honking or driving aggressively toward bison won’t make them move faster. In fact, it may have the opposite effect. NPS photos

posts.c: One of the things I find most extraordinary about polar bears is the immense journeys they undertake over a lifetime. Guided by a sense of smell seven times more powerful than a blood hound’s, they can detect a seal hidden beneath layers of snow and ice from more than half a mile away. They spend much of their lives following invisible trails of scent across hundreds of miles of Arctic wilderness. This is also how they find one another across a vast, seemingly desolate landscape, although finding mates has become more of a challenge as sea ice recedes. They are the great nomads of the Arctic, always inquisitive, resourceful, and, above all, fiercely determined to navigate a formidable and ever-changing world. For those interested in owning one of my polar bear prints, please visit the link in my bio or visit my website to submit an inquiry. From now until Christmas, all fine art purchases come with a copy of my new book Reverence.

posts.c: It's #NationalBisonDay, and we've got some bison facts! 1️⃣ Bison are the largest land mammal in North America Male bison (bulls) weigh up to 2,000 pounds and stand 6 feet tall, while females (cows) weigh up to 1,000 pounds and reach a height of 4-5 feet. Bison calves can weigh 30–70 pounds at birth. 2️⃣ Bison may be big, but they're also fast They are extremely agile and can run up to 30 miles per hour! 3️⃣ You can judge a bison's mood by its tail When it hangs down and swishes naturally, the bison is usually calm. If the tail is standing straight up, watch out! It may be ready to charge. No matter what a bison's tail is doing though, remember that they are unpredictable and can charge at any moment. Every year, there are regrettable accidents caused by people getting too close to these massive animals. It's great to love the bison but always be sure to love them from a distance of at least 25 yards (23 meters). 4️⃣ Bison love a good salad They primarily eat grasses, weeds and leafy p

posts.c: Climb ev’ry mountain, Gnaw ev’ry tree, The summit is calling, Living the porcupine dream. Porcupines are creatures of habit. They can spend days hanging out in the same tree, nibbling on bark and needles and quite content with their accommodations. But this particular porcupine has other plans. Not content to keep its paws at lower elevations, it’s steadily making its way uphill, navigating rocks and small plants with the determination of someone who has decided the grass really is greener higher up. Perhaps there’s a better tree waiting at the top. Perhaps it’s simply looking for a change of scenery. What we do know is that this porcupine is going places….mostly uphill. Perhaps to find its dream. NPS video/R. Buchanan: A porcupine walks uphill amid rocks and small plants @mountrainiernps Music of Climb every mountain plays.

posts.c: Ocean in Motion / La Danza del Mar invites the young and young at heart to connect with ocean life through movement and play. The ocean moves us! Hold on like a seahorse—there are plenty of them here and so much more to discover! Just swipe left and sea. African penguins are back in a newly expanded habitat! Watch as they groom and dive off the rocks. Then, practice your penguin waddle in this new interactive space. A 20-foot-long coral reef includes giant clams and a bluespotted ribbontail ray that glides along the sand. Nearby, clownfish nestle into anemones. Enjoy multiple play areas that are welcoming to visitors of all ages. There’s also plenty of rest areas to relax and check out the ocean views of Monterey Bay! Watch leaping blennies hop across wet stones! Visitors can also follow shapes in the floor to hop from rock to rock like blennies. There’s so much to discover in Ocean in Motion / La Danza del Mar from flamboyant cuttlefish to garden eels. Swim over to the link in bio for

posts.c: If you want to try a ribbon chain garland for the holidays, one of the best parts is how easy they are to store! ✨🌈 I literally throw them in the top of a storage bin. Make sure they’re loose and not smashed. They come out wrinkle free and ready to go for another year! Paper will not store this nicely! For these, I used 1.5” wide grosgrain ribbon. Each piece is cut to 8”. This will be my third year using these and they’re still in perfect shape 🙌🏻 Would you try these in your home? They’re so fun for the room the Christmas tree is in! 🎄

Home Ice Advantage, Higher Ground, and Striations of Time. As the holidays approach, my thoughts keep returning to Antarctica and how the continent must be stirring to life. With the polar summer fast approaching, Adélie and chinstrap penguins are building their nests and laying eggs. Icebergs sculpted by millennia of densely-packed snowfall glow blue beneath the returning light and provide young penguins refuge from leopard seals. It is one of the most spectacular sights in the world, though I also cannot help thinking of how long it will last between a changing climate and commercial fisheries exploiting its waters. My hope in sharing images like the ones above is that we recognize the beauty of what is at stake and take action to protect it. To inquire about prints and explore more of my work across the poles, visit the link in my bio. From now until Christmas, all fine art purchases come with a copy of my book Reverence.

posts.c: Hubble (along with ground-based telescopes) revealed that the expansion rate of our universe is accelerating! Soon, the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope will study the “dark energy” behind this expansion with its large field of view and infrared vision. Its treasure trove of data will include tens of thousands of exploding stars and hundreds of millions of distant galaxies, tracing the universe’s expansion across nearly all of cosmic history! Hubble's key observations led to dark energy's discovery (even helping earn a Nobel prize in physics!) and the mission will work with Roman to continue investigating this enigma. As we gear up for its first images, we'll share more here on how Roman and Hubble bring different superpowers to astronomy. Check the link in our bio for more! #NASA #Hubble #Roman #astrophysics #space

posts.c: Warm fall days mean more time on the trails, and at Catamount Outdoor Family Center, we love to see it! 🍂 Before you head home, make a quick tick check for you and your family a routine. Ticks stay active in the fall, especially on milder days, and they can be tiny. Here are some tips to help protect yourself this fall: 🧦 Dress for it: wear light-colored long pants and long sleeves, and tuck your pants into your socks before heading out. 🔍 Check the hard-to-see places: your scalp, behind your ears, your armpits, behind your knees, and your waistband. 👕 Toss your clothes in the dryer for 10 minutes on high heat when you get home. 🚿 Shower as soon as you’re done outside for the day. 🐾 Don’t forget to check your kids, gear, and pets too! Learn more at HealthVermont.gov/BeTickSmart. Come prepared and head home tick-free. Happy trails! 👣 #CatamountCommunity #TickAware #GetOutside #OutdoorRecreation #Vermont #Hike #Bike #Run #Walk

You've likely heard of geysers and hot springs, but what about fumaroles? Fumaroles (or steam vents) are the hottest hydrothermal features in Yellowstone, with temperatures up to 280 F (138 C)! 🔥 Because they are so hot and contain very little water, the water boils away before reaching the surface. Then, steam and other gases emerge from the feature's vent, sometimes making hissing or whistling sounds. Roaring Mountain is a wonderful place to enjoy the sights and sounds of fumaroles, especially on cooler days! 👉 Learn more about fumaroles at: go.nps.gov/YELLhydrothermalfeatures (link in our "Learn More" highlight) Photo (NPS / Ashton Hooker): Roaring Mountain on a chilly winter day.

posts.c: When choosing the images for my book Reverence, I let go of the photojournalist mindset honed over decades of working as a National Geographic photographer and looked instead for the images that sparked some kind of emotion within. The Falkland Islands (Islas Malvinas) are truly a place of extremes, battered by powerful, nutrient-dense currents that pummel the cliffs and feed the towering kelp forests below the surface. The density of life here is staggering, especially on Steeple Jason where conservationists had the foresight to reclaim the island from sheep farming as far back as the 70s. Today the island is under the guardianship of the Wildlife Conservation Society and its natural legacy is preserved as one of the last wild places on Earth.

posts.c: My BBC story on Quebecois profanity has its very own content warning — and some extremely NSFW French-language cursing. (Which I've been obsessed with since I was a baby linguist at Berkeley.) Quebec is "the Amazon rainforest of swear words," according to one expert, a reference to a lexicon so large, varied and colorful it outstrips most of the planet's 7,000-odd languages. I'm grateful to editor extraordinaire @eliot.stein for letting me write about my favorite foul-mouthed neighbors to the north, whose vocabulary is far better suited to recent political shenanigans than anything English can produce. ("Ostie consacrée au cul de cochon" is now my official position on this "51st state" business.) Thanks to the linguistics, historians, and experts — including @frenchwithfrederic and Michelle Bélanger of @museepop in Trois-Rivières — who spoke with me for the piece. And many thanks to the patrons of the wonderful Bar Sainte-Angèle for providing a few juicy exemplars during a recent visit

What if your fence could grow food instead of just taking up space? A fruit fence turns a simple vertical structure into a productive growing system, and passion fruit is perfect for the job because its climbing tendrils naturally grip onto nearby supports. The science is pretty cool. Passion fruit vines grow rapidly, spreading their leaves across a trellis to capture sunlight for photosynthesis. With enough light, water, and nutrients, the plant converts that energy into vigorous growth and eventually flowers and fruit. Training the vines vertically also helps you use space more efficiently, turning an otherwise unused area into productive growing space. And here’s the best part: a well-established passion fruit vine can produce an impressive harvest while giving you a living privacy screen. Instead of building a fence that only blocks the view, why not grow one that hides the eyesores, adds greenery, and produces delicious fruit? That’s a whole lot more value from the same footprint.

posts.c: Hello again, M30! This new image shows a globular star cluster, which is a roughly spherical grouping of stars held together by gravity. Because of Hubble's long life, it's been able to observe M30 multiple times and track how different populations of stars in globular clusters move. Hubble can discern incredibly specific details in distant objects, allowing for this unprecedented "long-form" astronomy. Discover more at the link in our bio! Image description: A star cluster seen up close, filling the view with thousands of stars. They are clearly divided between blue ones, which are scattered around the outskirts of the image but more towards the center and are the majority in the bright core of the cluster, and yellow stars, which are present in the core but make up most of the cluster outside of that. A few orange stars are closer to us and appear noticeably larger. Image credit: ESA/Hubble & NASA, M. Libralato, G. Piotto, A. Sarajedini #NASA #Hubble #news #stars #space
posts.hd: Hubble image of globular star cluster M30

posts.c: A season of low rain can turn an island into a beach… come explore! ☀️ The Colchester Causeway is a famous rec path that carves through Lake Champlain. It’s usually surrounded on all sides by water, but not this year. A dry summer and fall have left a “beach” between the rail trail and Law Island. ⭐️ Law Island is located about half a mile from where the Causeway meets the bay. Most of the bay has some water right now, but the area around the island is dry. You can walk or bike right to it! Last year, Vermont had a historic drought that dropped the lake by 8 feet. This was the first time in 72 years that the lake lost this much water. I posted two videos that went viral of the “islands” at Kill Kare State Park and Colchester Causeway. We were all in shock that we could walk to these islands! 🐠 Now, a year later, it feels surreal to walk to Law Island again. I didn’t feel the same sense of “adventure” as last year… maybe because the media told us this would be a “once in a lifetime” thi

posts.c: Small plants need love too! So I try to find a fun way to style them instead of just placing them in a standard terra cotta pot. Here, I took this 4” birkin philodendron and cut the perfect piece of cork to surround its roots. Instead of glue a stainless steel mesh base to the cork, like I typically do, I used a low planter to work as the base of the “pot” to hold in the soil. Obviously it has drainage holes for those that were about to ask 😉 I then dressed up the topsoil with live moss and called it a day. It might be small but it makes a strong statement 💚🌿 #plants #plantstyling #design #beforeandafter #babygirl Low planter from @fayraystudio

posts.c: Have you ever wondered how birds stay warm during winter? Chickadees grow feathers that can keep them up to 100 degrees F warmer than the surrounding air temperature. Waterfowl exhibit counter-current heat exchange in their limbs, which enables them to stand in cold water. Other adaptations include roosting with heads tucked into back feathers to conserve heat and staying active by retrieving food stored during the autumn months. 👉 Want to learn more? Visit the link in our “Learn More” highlight! Photos (NPS / Jim Peaco & Jacob W. Frank): (1) Mountain chickadee (2) Mallards on Alum Creek

posts.c: Each fall, landlocked Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar) leave the open waters of Lake Champlain and make their way upstream, navigating currents and rocky riverbeds to reach their spawning grounds. Often referred to as a salmon run, this seasonal journey takes place in rivers throughout the Lake Champlain watershed, including the Ausable, Boquet, and Winooski rivers. Beginning in early September and continuing through mid-November, this remarkable event is made challenging by barriers to movement and habitat degradation. The future of landlocked Atlantic salmon depends on our ability to restore and protect the river corridors essential to their survival. Read our full Lake Look column - An Upriver Journey - through the link in our bio🔗

posts.c: The ultimate group project: studying worlds beyond our own. As we get closer to the first images from the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, a long list of science objectives await. One way Roman will team up with Hubble is by the different ways the missions will study exoplanets. An exoplanet is a planet that orbits a star other than our Sun. Roman will likely find hundreds of thousands exoplanets with its remarkable instruments; meanwhile, Hubble’s capabilities allow for analysis of exoplanet atmospheres. This work is part of NASA's search for life elsewhere in the universe. Plus, Roman's coronograph instrument will be able to directly image some larger exoplanets. We'll share more here on how Roman and Hubble bring different superpowers to astronomy in the weeks to come. Check the link in our bio for more on Hubble and Roman! posts.c: We don’t need another reason to love creativity, but research linking arts participation to slower biological aging is a pretty good one. 🎨 A recent University College London study found that more frequent engagement in arts and cultural activities was associated with slower biological aging. Weekly arts participants showed a 4% slower pace of aging than those who rarely participated. Here’s why this matters for play. Art is one way we play. When we paint, dance, make music, experiment with materials, or create something alongside others, we’re engaging in the very things that make play powerful: curiosity, imagination, expression, and exploration. The research gives us another reason to take these experiences seriously. Play isn’t just entertainment or a break from real life. It’s part of how we nurture our creativity, connection, and vitality. Make something. Move something. Try something new. Give yourself the gift ofplay. #PlayIntention #PowerOfPlay #CreativeWellbeing #ArtsAndHealt
posts.cp: We don’t need another reason to love creativity, but research linking arts participation to slower biological aging is a pretty good one

posts.c: One of the densest concentrations of geysers in Yellowstone can be found in the remote Shoshone Geyser Basin, on the west side of Shoshone Lake. We visit the area in the latest Yellowstone Volcano Observatory monthly video update. 🌊 Shoshone Geyser Basin is one of the most spectacular in all of Yellowstone National Park. Located deep in the backcountry along the west side of Shoshone Lake, the area has one of the densest concentrations of geysers, second only to the Upper Geyser Basin (where Old Faithful is located). There are over 100 geysers in this region and 40 or 50 might be active at any given time. A trail takes you right by Minute Man geyser (always at the ready!), so it is quite easy to watch the frequent eruptions there. ⚡During the month of October 2026, the University of Utah Seismograph Stations, which monitors and operates the Yellowstone seismic network, located 66 earthquakes. The largest was a Magnitude 2.0. Throughout 2026, there has been very little change in ground

posts.c: A little throwback to my broke college girl dinner era…. Honestly, I forgot how good these things are. Basically everything you want in a pizza, minus having to make an actual pizza. And yes, they’re still just as good as they were at 1AM in college. Here’s how I made them: - Split English muffins in half, drizzle with EVOO, sprinkle with garlic powder, and bake at 400°F for about 10–12 minutes, until lightly golden. - Add marinara, mozzarella, provolone, (or whatever your favorite cheese is!), dried oregano, and a little garlic salt. - Back into the oven until the cheese is melted and bubbly. - Serve with extra warm marinara for dipping. Please tell me I’m not the only one who lived on these back in the day….

posts.c: Where's the oxygen? After researchers studied 37 nearby dwarf galaxies, they realized much of the oxygen they expected to see was missing. Oxygen is the main element formed by stars, and also the most abundant element after hydrogen and helium. But by using Hubble, these scientists learned that dwarf galaxies can only hang on to a small fraction of the oxygen made by stars. Energy from the low-mass galaxies’ massive stars, along with galactic winds unleashed by supernova explosions, are apparently more effective at driving out the oxygen than current models predict. Read more at the link in our bio! posts.c: I wish they had the slightest idea that how much they mean to us. Just yesterday, one of our cats disappeared out of sight for a few minutes as I’d left her chilling in the backyard. These are indoor cats, so they have absolutely zero clue about life beyond the four walls of our home & the little garden they know so well. And in those few moments, I went through an entire range of emotions. From panic to worry, from imagining all sorts of terrible possibilities to the fear of not knowing where she had gone. Meanwhile, 🐈 walked back in, completely unbothered, after her antics. 🤦🏻‍♀️ Also, as a cat owner, if there’s one thing I could recommend, it would be investing in a self-cleaning litter box. It has genuinely changed our lives, especially in a multi-cat household. posts.c: The stars are just the night sky's mice... The first image is Webb's near-infrared view of the Cat's Head Nebula, a star-forming region. Webb can see through the opaque clouds of dust and gas to see the stars forming within. One of these makes up the cat's glowing "eye" and another, with Webb's characteristic eight-pointed diffraction spikes, its whiskers. The second slide shows Webb's mid-infrared look at the Cat's head, the dust shining brightly. There are structures to the left of the cat visible in the infrared that do not appear in @NASAHubble's visible light view (third slide). The cat's eye is reddish here, glowing from inside the dust. The bright yellow ridge along the cat's "chest" shows gas illuminated and ionized by ultraviolet radiation from nearby massive stars. Happy Halloween! Credits: Image: NASA, ESA, STScI; Image Processing: Joseph DePasquale (STScI) Read more at the link in our bio. Image description in comments.

posts.c: Here’s looking at you, kid 👀👀👀👀 This Brazilian Whiteknee Tarantula is native to tropical areas of Brazil. Tarantula hair is adapted to help them sense vibrations and other stimuli, and some hairs are even barbed and can be used as a defensive mechanism. Many of us know tarantulas for their eight legs and two body segments, but there are other features that are characteristic of arachnids. If you look at a tarantula’s mouthparts, for instance, you will see chelicerae (jaw-like parts tipped with fangs) and a pair of pedipalps, which help them taste and hold their food. #tarantula #sandiegozoo

posts.c: Comment ‘dad’ on this post for an extra dad joke straight to your DM’s 👇 Cars use several types of filters to protect their engines, improve performance, and keep passengers comfortable. Air filters prevent dust and dirt from entering the engine, oil filters remove contaminants from engine oil, and fuel filters stop impurities from reaching the fuel system. These filters help reduce wear, improve efficiency, and extend the lifespan of important components. Cabin air filters also clean the air entering the passenger compartment, trapping dust, pollen, and other airborne particles. Interestingly, a clogged filter can reduce engine performance, restrict airflow, or cause unpleasant smells inside the car, depending on which filter is affected. Regular filter replacement is one of the simplest ways to keep a vehicle running smoothly.

posts.c: If you ask us, the longline tuna fishery in Hawaii is making waves! 🐟🌺 Solid fishery management can make even the less-selective fishing methods more ocean-friendly. Hawaii is leading the charge by making its longline fishery more environmentally sustainable. This means: ✅ switching from less than 20% human observer coverage to 100% electronic camera monitoring by 2027 to track bycatch and gather data for fishery management decisions. ✅ training fishers to safely handle and release accidentally caught species like sharks, turtles, seabirds, and marine mammals. ✅ gear modifications to reduce seabird interactions. ✅ strategic area closures to protect vulnerable species. and more! The future for longline tuna fishing in Hawaii is bright.☀️ Look for yellow- and green-rated tuna caught in Hawaii for your next sustainable meal. What is making this sea of sand march inland? ⌛ This timelapse shows the Lençóis Maranhenses National Park in northeastern Brazil, known for its large sand dunes and seasonal rainwater lagoons. Strong winds from the Atlantic Ocean keep these dunes in constant motion. Over the years, the wind steadily pushes the sand, causing the dunes to migrate inland and change the shape of the landscape. Satellite data helps scientists track how remote landscapes change over time. Captured by the joint @nasa and @usgs Landsat program, these natural-color images show over four decades of this moving environment. Video description: A natural-color Landsat time series of Brazil’s Lençóis Maranhenses National Park spanning from 1984 to 2026. As the video plays, large white sand dunes move steadily inland across the coast. Among the shifting white sand are darker patches of seasonal rainwater lagoons and vegetation. #nasa #earth #science

posts.c: How do you think you’d fare in a bathroom with zero storage? Be honest.⠀ ⠀ We designed and remodeled this bathroom for good friends who are self-proclaimed minimalists. And, having now built them a primary bathroom without a vanity or medicine cabinet, we can confirm: they are committed to the bit.⠀ ⠀ The absolute hero of this project is the marble sink. The veining. The buttery soft texture. Those slender chrome legs… It’s gorgeous. ⠀ ⠀ We considered putting a cabinet below it, but it felt kind of like buying an amazing outfit only to wear your winter coat in every photograph. The cabinet idea was out. Instead, we used a couple of shelves over the toilet… for friends who can look at a little wicker basket and respect its capacity.⠀ ⠀ There’s something wonderful about designing for people who know exactly how they want to live. They wanted less stuff and a beautiful bathroom. ⠀ ⠀ They got both.⠀ ⠀ Design, Build, Photography @renovationhusbands⠀ Hardware & Sink @rejuvenation⠀ Tile @thet

posts.c: We’re not kitten around! @NASAHubble and @NASAWebb captured a purr-fect view of the Cat’s Head Nebula. This long thin structure, made of dark, dense dust, looks like the head of a cat, its eye a newborn star still shrouded by the dust and gas from which it formed. Hubble and Webb’s contrasting and complementary views give us a fuller picture of the features of this object. In the mid-infrared, as seen by Webb, the dust shines brightly while in the near-infrared, Webb can see through the dust to the stars hidden within. In visible light, Hubble's view shows a dark brown pillar of dust, with a yellow ridge along the right side. This bright rim shows gas illuminated and ionized by ultraviolet radiation from nearby massive stars. On the left are some dust pillars seen in the mid-infrared that are not observed in visible light. It's paw-sible to "fly through" these views with the help of visualizations created by (human) data scientists, which bring Hubble and Webb observations to un-fur-ge

posts.c: Higher waters, warmer waters, bluer waters El Niño is a natural weather pattern that occurs roughly every two to seven years and the one we’re experiencing now is on track to be the strongest on record. While El Niño occurs in the Pacific Ocean, with changes most visible along the equator, its effects can be felt all around the world. NASA satellites like PACE and Sentinel-6 are equipped to measure some of the key features of the phenomenon. Video description: Three data visualizations stacked vertically show sea surface height, sea surface temperature, and ocean color from January 2026 to September 2026. As it plays, text forms across the screen that reads “We’re experiencing a record El Niño” and transitions to “Swipe to compare the growing 2026 El Niño with a weak La Niña in 2025.” Higher waters, warmer waters, bluer waters El Niño is a natural weather pattern that occurs roughly every two to seven years and the one we’re experiencing now is on track to be the strongest on record. posts.c: Hardneck garlic relies on a process called vernalization, where prolonged exposure to cold temperatures triggers the physiological changes needed for proper bulb development. Without enough chilling, the plant may grow leaves but struggle to form the full, well-developed bulbs you want. Refrigerating hardneck garlic for about two months can help simulate winter, even in a warm climate. That cold exposure influences the plant’s growth signals, helping prepare it for the transition into active growth once temperatures rise. It’s essentially giving the garlic the seasonal cue it needs, without having to live somewhere with an actual winter. Once you plant those chilled cloves, they can resume growth with the cold requirement better satisfied, improving the chances of developing well-formed bulbs. It’s a great example of how understanding a plant’s biology lets you work around your climate instead of being limited by it.

posts.c: Hanging peppers might look like an old-school gardening trick, but there’s some cool science behind it. When you hang peppers to dry, moisture gradually evaporates from their skin and inner tissues into the surrounding air. The key is airflow and low humidity, which help carry that moisture away so the peppers can dry more efficiently. As their water content drops, it becomes harder for many spoilage microbes to grow, helping preserve your harvest for longer. Here’s why the way you string them matters, too. Threading through the calyx, the leafy cap at the top of the pepper, helps avoid puncturing the fleshy fruit, where damaged tissue and trapped moisture can encourage rot. Give your peppers a dry, well-ventilated spot, and you’re using evaporation and moisture control to turn a fresh harvest into a longer-lasting supply of homegrown heat.

The horseshoe-shaped island is actually the exposed part of a volcano itself, while the harbor in its center is a phantom of that massive volcanic eruption. As the volcano’s magma chamber emptied, the sudden drop in pressure inside the volcano caused the top to collapse and form a caldera — now called Port Foster. The thin arch of rock comes to a ridge that runs the length of the island, along its center, like a backbone. posts.c: We asked this 8-year-old to draw the famous “Cosmic Cliffs” hidden within the Carina Nebula, based on the famous James Webb Space Telescope image. The region is actually the edge of a gigantic, gaseous cavity within NGC 3324, roughly 7,600 light-years away. The cavernous area has been carved from the nebula by the intense ultraviolet radiation and stellar winds from extremely massive, hot, young stars located in the center of the bubble, above the area shown in this image. The high-energy radiation from these stars is sculpting the nebula’s wall by slowly eroding it away. Our artist managed to capture the beauty of this Webb image, along with her version of the telescope itself, a rocket ship, and there is even a cameo of "The Traveler" exploring the cosmos! I imagine I’ll find my way back to mt airy since I love her so much, but for now I’m back in the city and excited to decorate my new solo (!!!) apt and for all that comes next 💖

Optical illusions happen because your eyes send information to your brain, and your brain immediately starts making educated guesses about what it is seeing. Usually that works perfectly, but certain patterns, colors, shadows, and shapes can trick those shortcuts, making still images appear to move or identical lines look completely different. The best part is that even after someone explains the illusion, your brain may still refuse to cooperate. You can literally know two squares are the same color and your brain will look you dead in the eye and say, “No, they absolutely are not.” Like this content? Follow us for more @dadsaysjokes ❤️

Sen. Bernie Sanders said Tuesday he would not be supporting Sen. Chuck Schumer as the Democratic majority leader in the new Congress, setting up a seismic confrontation after the party’s sweep to power in the midterm elections. Sanders was joined by Democratic Sen. Elissa Slotkin of Michigan at a news conference at the Capitol, and together they said there needs to be a new generation of leadership and a vigorous debate about the party's direction and future. A number of incoming Democratic senators have echoed the call, signaling that they would support another candidate over Schumer. “The time is now for change,” said Sanders, the independent from Vermont and essentially the father of modern progressivism in the U.S. “And I will not be supporting Chuck to be reelected as the Democratic leader.” Read the full story at the link in our bio. held.c: Last week was tough for us. We were about to go on our daily walk, Kiki was on the couch while I put her harness on, I quickly went upstairs, and when I came back down, she was laying on the floor acting strange. When she got up, she was panting, drooling, and lifting her paw. It was 4pm on a Sunday, which meant the vets were closed. We had to drive 25 minutes to an emergency vet, they gave her pain meds and told us to keep an eye on her. On Monday morning, she was visibly in pain - as you can see in the first few clips. So we took her to the vet again. They told us - she has no noticeable fractures so you can either wait it out with her pain meds, or do an xray to find out more. We wanted to know more. And thank goodness we did… as it turned out, Kiki had hip dysplasia. One that you can tell it has most likely been there since she was a puppy - some dogs get it genetically. held.c: Ok people, It is Election Day and I hope you all know what that means! Time to go VOTE!! If you are like me, you may be saddened by the current political state in our country. Party allegiance aside, so much of what is being talked about seems to be fueled by hatred, violence and struggle. While It can all feel overwhelming, I always try and remember that the actual people who live in this country are loving, kind, hard working and resilient. When I was greeted with the above spread I was reminded about how great the people are and how important It is to elect leaders who think and act like us. The vast majority of us still do things because It helps to lift up our people, not because It is going to make us a billion dollars. This Election Day I will vote for the hard working Americans who deserve a better and easier path forward, and I will vote against the greedy and power obsessed billionaires who think they can run this country. Shoutout to whoever dialed in these cider doughnuts,

It’s Pop-up week 🔍 What exactly is “slow looking”? Slow looking is an approach to viewing art that emphasizes our own observations and reflections, rather than familiarity with the artwork or art terminology. It’s also a visual thinking strategy used by first-year medical students in Dr. Sakshi Jasra’s Professionalism, Communication, and Reflection class at the Larner College of Medicine. Now in it’s third year running with the Fleming, we partnered with Dr. Jasra to transform her popular assignment into a pop-up exhibit for all! Now through Saturday, visit the Learning Studio to visit “Double Take” any time during our regular hours and try slow looking for yourself. Featuring a wide range of works from our collections, including a clay tablet from Mesopotamia, a photograph by Carrie Mae Weems, and much more, simply choose a work and follow our prompts. The only thing you need to bring is your own curiosity.

After 38 wonderful years, The Vermont Pub & Brewery is sadly closing our doors. Since 2020, we’ve struggled to get back to the level of business that is necessary to sustain our operation, and unfortunately we just don’t have the resources to hold out any longer for that day to come. Our last full day of service will be Saturday, November 14th, three days after our 38th anniversary on November 11th. We owe a debt of gratitude to our beloved staff, past and present, as well as a myriad of regular patrons, many of whom have been coming in since day one! We are honored to have been a part of your lives for so many years, and we will truly miss you all. Greg's legacy does not end with the closing of VPB, but he will live on in our hearts and in every sip of Vermont craft beer and beyond. Stay tuned for upcoming beer and food specials!

In loving memory of my bestest friend and the light of my life, Jax. Rescued by PETA in 2010 at a year old, he was my shadow for the next 16+ years, sharing adventures and cuddles. His big brown eyes could stare into my soul and his big ears heard everything. He had quite the personality and loved to “talk,” and I quickly learned to understand his squeaks and groans. Jax was an excellent travel companion, happy to just be wherever I was. He was a master sunbather, always searching for the coziest spot in the house to catch some rays. In his younger years he loved to hike (and later enjoyed riding along in a backpack), and he was always ready to chase tennis balls or play tug-o’ -war until we were both exhausted. Then, he’d cuddle up next to me under a blanket, burrow his nose in, and snore and dream. At the end, with his face and muzzle nearly white, he was declining quickly and ready to go, and I was grateful to be able to give him a peaceful goodbye. Life isn’t the same without him,
held.cp: In loving memory of my bestest friend and the light of my life, Jax
